question.text: Scenario: Mr. Ramesh is 55 years old and has been employed with a manufacturing company for 28 years. His current basic salary is Rs. 80,000 per month and dearness allowance (DA) is Rs. 20,000 per month. He is covered under the Payment of Gratuity Act. His EPF balance stands at Rs. 45,00,000 (employee share Rs. 22,00,000, employer share Rs. 23,00,000). He also has an NPS Tier I account with a total corpus of Rs. 32,00,000 (own contributions: Rs. 16,00,000) and a superannuation fund with Rs. 18,00,000. His employer contributes 12% to EPF, 10% of basic+DA to NPS, and Rs. 1,50,000 annually to the superannuation fund. He plans to retire at age 60. He has never taken an NPS partial withdrawal before. Question 1 of 5: Mr. Ramesh wishes to take a partial withdrawal from his EPF at age 55 for pre-retirement purposes. Based on the EPF pre-retirement partial withdrawal rules, which of the following is correct?

answer.text: 90% of the total EPF balance = 90% x Rs. 45,00,000 = Rs. 40,50,000
90% of the employee's share = 90% x Rs. 22,00,000 = Rs. 19,80,000
75% of the total EPF balance = 75% x Rs. 45,00,000 = Rs. 33,75,000

He cannot take the 90% pre-retirement withdrawal yet because the facility is available only within one year of retirement or superannuation, and at age 55 with retirement planned at 60 he is outside that window

explanation.text: The Logic: EPF allows a pre-retirement partial withdrawal of up to 90% of the total EPF balance (both employee and employer shares) once the member has attained age 54 AND the withdrawal is within one year of actual retirement or superannuation. Mr. Ramesh has crossed the age 54 threshold, but with retirement planned at age 60, he is still about five years away from retirement, so the within-one-year-of-retirement condition is not satisfied. The Trap: Candidates often focus only on the age 54 condition and conclude that 90% of the total balance can be withdrawn the moment that age is reached. The rule has two conjunctive conditions, age (>= 54) and proximity to retirement (within one year). The 75% figure relates to a different withdrawal route (post-unemployment withdrawal of 75% after one month of unemployment) and does not apply here. Note: The pre-retirement 90% withdrawal becomes available to Mr. Ramesh only when he is within one year of his planned retirement at age 60. Until then, other EPF withdrawal heads (illness, housing, etc.) operate under their own separate limits and conditions.
